`trust()` minimizes the objective function $\ell(\theta)$, $-2 \log L$ or $-2 \log$ of the posterior, by a trust-region
method on the exact gradient [@kaschek2019dmod]. Arguments and usage:
[Optimization](guide-optimization.html).

## Trust-region method

At the iterate $\theta_k$ with the gradient $b = \nabla \ell(\theta_k)$ and a symmetric approximation $H$ of the Hessian,
`trust()` minimizes the [quadratic model]{#def-quadratic-model} $m(s)$ of the change of $\ell$
along a step $s$, the second-order Taylor polynomial with $H$ in place of the Hessian, inside the
[trust region]{#def-trust-region}, a ball of [radius]{#def-radius} $r$,

$$\min_{s} \; m(s) = b^\top s + \tfrac{1}{2}\, s^\top H s \quad \text{subject to} \quad
  \lVert s \rVert \le r . \tag{1}$$

The ratio of actual to predicted decrease $-m(s)$ decides on the step and the radius $r$. Subproblem,
radius, bounds and termination are the same for every source of $H$ and on the
[sparse path](#sparse-hessians).

### Trust-region subproblem

`trust()` solves the [subproblem]{#def-subproblem} (1), the minimization of the quadratic model over
the trust region, once per iteration and exactly, through the full eigendecomposition of $H$
[@more1983computing]. The solution satisfies $(H + \nu I)\, s = -b$ with a [multiplier]{#def-multiplier} $\nu \ge 0$,
the Lagrange multiplier of the radius constraint, that makes $H + \nu I$ positive semidefinite and vanishes unless the step reaches the boundary,
$\lVert s \rVert = r$. With $H = Q \Lambda Q^\top$, eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ and $\gamma = Q^\top b$,
the step

$$s(\nu) = -Q (\Lambda + \nu I)^{-1} \gamma \tag{2}$$

solves the subproblem when $\nu \ge \max(0, -\lambda_{\min})$ and either $\nu = 0$ with
$\lVert s \rVert \le r$, or $\nu > 0$ with $\lVert s \rVert = r$. The second case is a root of the
[secular equation]{#def-secular-equation}, which sets $\nu$ such that the step ends on the boundary,

$$\begin{aligned}
\phi(\nu) &= \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{\lVert s(\nu) \rVert} \\
 &= \frac{1}{r} - \Big( \sum_i \frac{\gamma_i^2}{(\lambda_i + \nu)^2} \Big)^{-1/2},
\end{aligned} \tag{3}$$

nearly linear for $\nu > -\lambda_{\min}$, solved by bisection on a bracket of $\nu$, every
evaluation $O(n_\theta)$ in the eigenbasis. If $\gamma_i = 0$ for every eigenvector of
$\lambda_{\min} < 0$ and $\lVert s(-\lambda_{\min}) \rVert \le r$ ([hard case]{#def-hard-case}), the solution is
$s(-\lambda_{\min}) + \tau q_{\min}$ with $\lVert s \rVert = r$; otherwise it is the root of (3). Negative curvature is
followed to the boundary. The eigendecomposition costs $O(n_\theta^3)$; sparse Hessians use the
[sparse path](#sparse-hessians).

### Radius update

With the ratio of actual to predicted decrease

$$\rho_k = \frac{\ell(\theta_k) - \ell(\theta_k + s_k)}{-m_k(s_k)}, \tag{4}$$

the radius is updated with $r_{\max}$ = `rmax`:

$$r_{k+1} = \begin{cases}
\min(r_k/4,\, \lVert s_k \rVert / 4), & \rho_k < 1/4, \\
\min(2 r_k,\, r_{\max}), & \rho_k > 3/4 \text{ and } \lVert s_k \rVert \ge 0.9\, r_k, \\
r_k, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases} \tag{5}$$

A step with $\rho_k < 1/4$ is rejected. The radius grows only when the step reached the boundary.
Under `boundary = "clip"` the radius shrinks to $r_k/4$, grows at $\rho_k > 3/4$ after every step
that is not the Newton step, and a step that lowers $\ell$ is accepted where the value or model test ends the run.
The first radius is `rinit`. A trial point where the objective fails or is not finite counts as
rejected; three in a row end the run (`"objfun"`).

### Nonmonotone acceptance

With `stepControl$nonmonotone` $= \eta \in (0, 1)$,
[nonmonotone acceptance]{#def-nonmonotone-acceptance} measures the actual decrease from a
weighted average of past values [@zhang2004nonmonotone], so an accepted step may raise $\ell$,

$$\begin{aligned}
Q_{k+1} &= \eta Q_k + 1, \\
C_{k+1} &= \frac{\eta Q_k C_k + \ell(\theta_{k+1})}{Q_{k+1}},
\end{aligned} \tag{6}$$

updated at accepted steps, and $\rho_k$ is (4) with $C_k$ in place of $\ell(\theta_k)$;
$\eta = 0$ recovers (4).
The result is the best iterate visited; the termination tests read $\ell$ itself.

### Bound constraints

`boundary = "reflective"` is the interior method of Coleman and Li [@coleman1994convergence].
With
$v_i$ the signed distance to the bound in the descent direction $-b_i$ (1 if infinite),
$D = \operatorname{diag}(\lvert v \rvert^{1/2})$ and $J^v$ the diagonal of
$\partial \lvert v \rvert / \partial \theta$, the subproblem is solved in the scaled variables

$$\hat b = D b, \qquad \hat B = D H D + \operatorname{diag}(b)\, J^v . \tag{7}$$

The optimality measure of `gtol`, $\max_i \lvert v_i b_i \rvert$, vanishes at interior stationary
points and at active bounds. A step leaving the box is cut to the fraction
$\max(\texttt{thetaMax}, 1 - \text{optimality measure})$ of the distance (`thetaMax` = 0.99995),
reflected, or replaced by scaled steepest descent, whichever the model rates best. The ratio (4)
and the step length in (5) are those of the scaled model of (7).
`boundary = "clip"` removes active parameters from the subproblem and clips the step.

### Termination criteria

The tests are listed in [Optimization](guide-optimization.html#termination-criteria). Only
`"gradient"` tests optimality; `"fvalue"`, `"preddiff"` and `"step"` read the quadratic model and
can stop at a non-stationary point if $H$ is poor. A `"gradient"`, `"fvalue"` or `"preddiff"` stop
that ends the run also needs the full Newton step of the scaled model (7) at the current iterate to
predict a decrease of at most `mtol`,

$$\begin{aligned}
\tfrac{1}{2}\, \hat b^\top \hat B^{+} \hat b
 &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\hat\lambda_i > 0} \frac{(\hat q_i^\top \hat b)^2}{\hat\lambda_i} \\
 &\le \texttt{mtol} ,
\end{aligned} \tag{8}$$

with [$\hat B^{+}$]{#def-b-hat-plus} the inverse of $\hat B$ on the eigenvectors of positive
eigenvalues and zero on the others, the eigenpairs $(\hat\lambda_i, \hat q_i)$ of $\hat B$, and
eigenvalues inside the [noise floor]{#def-noise-floor} of the eigendecomposition, the rounding error
below which an eigenvalue is not resolved, counted as zero. Along a direction of curvature $\lambda$ the gradient at a
distance $d$ from the minimum is $\lambda d$ and the value lies $\lambda d^2 / 2$ above it, so a
small gradient along a flat direction does not mean a value close to the minimum; (8) bounds that
excess. On the [sparse path](#sparse-hessians) the Cholesky factors give (8) where $\hat B$ is
positive definite, the dense eigendecomposition of $\hat B$ elsewhere; `trustL1()` evaluates (8) on
the model of the coordinates not held at a kink ([L1 penalties](#l1-penalties)). A run that fails
(8) goes on, within `iterlim`; `mtol = 0` drops the condition. [Stagnation]{#def-stagnation}, five rejected steps in a
row that leave the value within `ftol`, ends the run, with `converged = TRUE` only where (8) holds:
where the noise of the value exceeds the decrease a step predicts, a non-stationary point
stagnates as well. While further phases follow, the
value, model and step tests hand over to the next one, unless the phase ends the run on them
([Hessian phases](#hessian-phases)); the last quasi-Newton phase therefore
ends only on the gradient, stagnation, the radius, `iterlim` or a failing objective
[@nocedal2006numerical]. For an ODE integrated at relative tolerance $\epsilon$ a weighted
residual $r_j$ of a prediction $g_j$ has an error of about $\epsilon g_j / \sigma_j$, so the value has one of about
$2 \epsilon \sum_j \lvert r_j g_j \rvert / \sigma_j$, growing with the amount of data, the gradient
more; `ftol` and `gtol` belong at or above these noise floors.

## Sources of the model Hessian

### Gauss-Newton approximation

The Hessian of $\sum_j r_j^2$ in the weighted residuals $r_j$ is the Gauss-Newton Hessian
$2 J^\top J$ plus a term with the second derivatives of the residuals
([Sensitivities and Hessians](methods-sensitivities.html#gradient-and-hessian-of-the-objective)).
Gauss-Newton keeps the first, positive semidefinite term, which comes free with the gradient; the
second is small where residuals scatter around zero. A Gaussian prior adds twice the prior precision on
the diagonal ([Likelihood and prior](methods-objective.html#prior)).
With a parameter-dependent error model the matrix is $J^\top L J$, not necessarily semidefinite
([Sensitivities and Hessians](methods-sensitivities.html#gauss-newton-with-an-error-model)). With
[large residuals]{#def-large-residual}, where the second term is not small, the Gauss-Newton model
can stop short of the minimum.

### Exact Hessian

`hessianMethod = "exact"` runs Newton's method in the trust region with second-order
sensitivities ([Sensitivities and Hessians](methods-sensitivities.html)), exact also for large
residuals and at a much higher cost per iteration.

### BFGS update

Both quasi-Newton updates use the secant pair

$$\begin{aligned}
s_k &= \theta_{k+1} - \theta_k, \\
y_k &= \nabla \ell(\theta_{k+1}) - \nabla \ell(\theta_k),
\end{aligned} \tag{9}$$

with the secant equation $B_{k+1} s_k = y_k$. BFGS keeps $B$ positive definite, which needs
$s^\top y > 0$; the pair is [damped]{#def-damping}, $y$ mixed with $B s$ [@powell1978fast]:

$$\begin{aligned}
\vartheta &= \begin{cases}
1, & s^\top y \ge 0.2\, s^\top B s, \\
\dfrac{0.8\, s^\top B s}{s^\top B s - s^\top y}, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases} \\
\tilde y &= \vartheta y + (1 - \vartheta) B s ,
\end{aligned} \tag{10}$$

the update is

$$B_{k+1} = B_k - \frac{B_k s\, s^\top B_k}{s^\top B_k s} + \frac{\tilde y\, \tilde y^\top}{s^\top \tilde y}. \tag{11}$$

Then $s^\top \tilde y \ge 0.2\, s^\top B s > 0$. The [cautious test]{#def-cautious-test} `qnCautious` skips pairs with
$s^\top y \le c \lVert s \rVert \lVert y \rVert$ (counted in `qnSkipped`). BFGS updates from
accepted steps only.

### SR1 update

SR1 satisfies the secant equation without definiteness. With $w = y - B_k s$,

$$B_{k+1} = B_k + \frac{w\, w^\top}{w^\top s}, \tag{12}$$

skipped when $\lvert w^\top s \rvert \le 10^{-8} \lVert s \rVert \lVert w \rVert$. SR1 approaches
the true Hessian, indefinite regions included. Rejected trial points also give valid pairs
[@nocedal2006numerical]; `qnRejected` (default for `"sr1"`) uses them.

### Structured secant updates

The data term of `normL2()` is a sum of row losses $\ell_i(m_i)$ in the prediction and sigma
$m_i$ of a data point, $\ell_i = r_i^2$ in the simplest case. With the Jacobian $J$ of all $m_i$
and the derivatives $u_i = \partial \ell_i / \partial m_i$, the gradient is $J^\top u$ and the
Hessian is the Gauss-Newton Hessian $G = J^\top L J$, $L$ the Hessian of the losses in $m$, which
the objective returns, plus $C = \sum_i u_i^\top \nabla^2 m_i$. The [structured secant updates]{#def-structured-secant-update} keep $G$
at every iterate and learn only $A \approx C$ from the steps. The secant of Dennis, Martínez and
Tapia [@dennis1989convergence] is $(J_{k+1} - J_k)^\top u_{k+1}$ for the data term, of
Gauss-Newton Hessian $G^{\rm LS}$; the other terms of a sum, such as a prior, take the secant of
their gradient and Hessian:

$$\begin{aligned}
B_k &= G_k + A_k, \\
y^\#_k &= y_k - J_k^\top (u_{k+1} - u_k) - \left(G_{k+1} - G^{\rm LS}_{k+1}\right) s_k ,
\end{aligned} \tag{13}$$

$s_k$ and $y_k$ from (9). For $\ell_i = r_i^2$, $u = 2 r$ and the data part is
$2 (J_{k+1} - J_k)^\top r_{k+1}$, as in Fides [@froehlich2022fides]. It equals
$C(\theta_{k+1}) s_k$ up to $O(\lVert s_k \rVert^2)$ and takes nothing from the linearization
error of $G$, which grows with the step where the residuals are nonlinear. A Gaussian prior,
whose Hessian is constant and part of $G$, adds nothing. Asked for `hessian = "structured"`, an
objective returns $J$, $u$ and $G^{\rm LS}$ (see `objlist()`); an objective without them has
$J = 0$ and $G^{\rm LS} = 0$ in (13).

`"sbfgs"` applies the BFGS update (11) with $\tilde y = y$ to $G_{k+1} + A_k$ with the pair
$(s_k, G_{k+1} s_k + y^\#_k)$ and keeps the difference to $G_{k+1}$,

$$A_{k+1} = \operatorname{BFGS}(G_{k+1} + A_k;\ s_k, G_{k+1} s_k + y^\#_k) - G_{k+1}, \tag{14}$$

after accepted steps and with the test of `qnCautious`. The update is not damped: $G_{k+1}$
changes from iterate to iterate, so $G_{k+1} + A_k$ need not be positive definite along $s_k$,
and the update then still restores the secant equation. `"ssr1"` applies (12) to the correction,

$$A_{k+1} = A_k + \frac{w\, w^\top}{w^\top s_k}, \qquad w = y^\#_k - A_k s_k, \tag{15}$$

skipped when $\lvert w^\top s_k \rvert \le 10^{-8} \lVert s_k \rVert \lVert w \rVert$. $A$ stays
indefinite where $C$ is, and rejected trial points update it under `qnRejected`. Both start at
$A_0 = 0$, so the first step is a Gauss-Newton step; a handover or a [reseed]{#def-reseed}, a restart of the update from a new seed, starts there again.
A pair that leaves $A$ unchanged counts in `qnSkipped`.

`qnScaling = "residual"` is the totally structured secant method of Huschens
[@yabe1998quadratic]. With the residual norm $\rho = \lVert u \rVert$, which is $2 \lVert r \rVert$
for $\ell_i = r_i^2$, and $\rho = \sqrt{\ell}$ for an objective without data rows,

$$B_k = G_k + \rho_k A_k, \qquad z_k = \frac{\rho_{k+1}}{\rho_k}\, y^\#_k , \tag{16}$$

(14) or (15) act on $\rho_{k+1} A_k$ with $z_k$ in place of $y^\#_k$, and $A_{k+1}$ is the
result divided by $\rho_{k+1}$. The correction vanishes with the residuals: convergence is
quadratic for a [zero residual]{#def-zero-residual}, an exact fit of the data at the minimum where
$C = 0$, and superlinear otherwise. $\rho = 0$ leaves $A$ unchanged.

`"gnsbfgs"` is the hybrid Gauss-Newton structured BFGS method of Zhou and Chen
[@zhou2010global]. After every accepted step, with $z_k$ from (16),

$$\begin{aligned}
B_{k+1} &= \begin{cases}
G_{k+1} + A_{k+1}, & z_k^\top s_k \ge \epsilon\, s_k^\top s_k , \\
G_{k+1}, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases} \\
A_{k+1} &= \begin{cases}
\operatorname{BFGS}(A_k;\ s_k, z_k), & z_k^\top s_k \ge \epsilon\, s_k^\top s_k , \\
A_k, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\end{aligned} \tag{17}$$

with $\epsilon$ = `qnHybridTol`, default $10^{-6}$ as in the paper, the undamped update (11) and
$A_0 = 0$. The ratio $z^\top s / s^\top s$ tends to zero for a zero residual, where the run becomes
Gauss-Newton with quadratic convergence, and stays above a positive bound where $C$ is positive
definite at the minimum, where the run is structured BFGS with superlinear convergence. The
Gauss-Newton branch is $G$ alone, since the trust region regularizes; `qnHybridShift = TRUE` adds
the term $\rho\, I$ of the paper, with the residual norm $\rho$ of (16), which keeps the matrix of
the line search positive definite there. Where $C$ is
indefinite at the minimum the ratio of a step can stay negative and the run then stays
Gauss-Newton. `"gnssr1"` uses (15) with $z_k$ and the test
$\lvert z_k^\top s_k \rvert \ge \epsilon\, s_k^\top s_k$, so it takes negative curvature into the
correction as well. In the trace `hessianSource` is `"gn"` for the iterations on the Gauss-Newton
branch, `hybridGN` counts the steps that chose it.

### Seed and memory

Far from the optimum $J^\top J$ is large and ill-conditioned; BFGS corrects a [seed]{#def-seed}, the matrix the update starts from, that is wrong
by orders of magnitude only slowly, SR1 overwrites it. With `qnMemory` $= m > 0$ the approximation
is rebuilt from $\gamma I$, $\gamma = y^\top y / s^\top y$ [@shanno1978matrix], and the last $m$
pairs, the curvature of L-BFGS [@nocedal2006numerical] as an explicit matrix. There is no
diagonal preconditioner: on the log scale the ill-conditioning of [sloppy models]{#def-sloppy-model}, whose Hessian eigenvalues spread evenly
over many orders of magnitude, lies along rotated directions [@gutenkunst2007universally].

### Hessian phases

A [phase]{#def-phase}, a part of the run with one source of $H$, [hands over]{#def-handover} to the next where a value, model, step or stagnation stop or the `iterlim` of the phase
would end the run; `"gradient"` ends the run, and with `onStop = "end"` the value, model, step and
stagnation stops end it as well. A phase with `radiusStall` $= n$ also hands over after $n$
consecutive iterations that leave the radius unchanged, an accepted step inside the region or one
that the region at `rmax` bounds. A handover resets the radius to `rinit`, or keeps it with
`keepRadius = TRUE`, and seeds a quasi-Newton phase with the Gauss-Newton Hessian at the iterate of
the handover. With `hessianInit = "tracked"` a BFGS phase starts instead from a matrix kept over the
whole run: the Hessian of the first phase at $\theta_0$, with the absolute values of the
eigenvalues where it is indefinite, updated by (10) and (11) with the pair (9) of every accepted step of the
phases before, under the same tests as the update in the phase.

The default of `trust()` is the hybrid method of Fides [@froehlich2022fides]: Gauss-Newton with
`radiusStall = 20` and `onStop = "end"`, then BFGS, tracked from the Gauss-Newton Hessian at
$\theta_0$, at the radius of the switch, which happens at most once. Where the residuals at the
minimum are large, the Gauss-Newton model misses the second term of the Hessian, and the
Gauss-Newton steps converge linearly, inside the region: the radius no longer changes, and the
BFGS matrix, which has taken up the curvature along the path, takes over. A run
that converges before 20 iterations at an unchanged radius stays Gauss-Newton throughout. The BFGS
phase evaluates the gradient forward, so the switch costs no evaluation. Multiple shooting,
`boundary = "clip"` and the [sparse path](#sparse-hessians) run Gauss-Newton alone, as
`hessianMethod = "gn"` does.

### Sparse Hessians

A sparse Hessian $H = S + U D U^\top$, $S$ sparse and the [low-rank part]{#def-low-rank-part} $U D U^\top$ of few columns $m$ in $U$ and the
diagonal $D$, dense curvature without a dense matrix, takes the same steps without the eigendecomposition. The root of (3) is found by Newton's
method on $1/\lVert s(\nu) \rVert$, safeguarded by a bracket of $\nu$, to a relative $10^{-12}$:
every iterate factorizes $S + \nu I$ by sparse Cholesky, with the ordering of one symbolic
analysis per pattern, and adds $U D U^\top$ by the Woodbury identity through
$K = D^{-1} + U^\top (S + \nu I)^{-1} U$. $H + \nu I$ is positive definite where $S + \nu I$ has
$p$ negative eigenvalues, $K$ has $q$ positive ones and $p + q$ equals the number of positive
entries of $D$; an indefinite $S + \nu I$ is factorized as $L \Delta L^\top$ for $p$. In the hard
case the eigenvector of $\lambda_{\min}$ comes from inverse iteration on the factor at $\nu$ next
to $-\lambda_{\min}$. `sparse = "auto"` compares the flops of a step, about eight factorizations
with $m + 2$ solves each from the symbolic analysis, with the $4 n_\theta^3$ of the
eigendecomposition.

A BFGS phase on the sparse path, `"bfgs"` with `hessianInit = "gn"`, is limited-memory BFGS on the
Hessian $B_0 = S_0 + U_0 D_0 U_0^\top$ of the objective at the start of the phase. It keeps the last
$m$ pairs (9), $m$ = `qnMemory` or 10 where that is 0, each damped by (10) against the model it
updates and skipped by the same tests as the dense update. In the compact representation
[@byrd1994representations]

$$\begin{aligned}
B &= B_0 - W M^{-1} W^\top, \qquad W = (B_0 S,\ Y), \\
M &= \begin{pmatrix} S^\top B_0 S & L \\ L^\top & -E \end{pmatrix},
\end{aligned} \tag{18}$$

$S$ and $Y$ hold the pairs as columns, $L$ the strict lower triangle of $S^\top Y$ and $E$ the
diagonal. With $M = P \Theta P^\top$ the correction joins the low-rank part as the $2m$ columns of
$W P$ with the diagonal $-\Theta^{-1}$, which has entries of both signs, so the sparse factor is that
of $S_0$ throughout the phase. $B_0$ stays fixed: the phase evaluates value and gradient only, and a
Hessian at every iterate would cost what the phase saves. A BFGS update keeps the inertia of the
matrix it starts from, so an indefinite $B_0$, the Gauss-Newton Hessian of an error model that
depends on the parameters for one, would keep the directions of negative curvature for the whole
phase. Where the factorization of $B_0$ shows it is not positive definite, $B_0$ takes $\tau I$
added, $\tau$ the smallest of $10^{-8}, 10^{-7}, \ldots$ times a bound of $\lVert B_0 \rVert$ that
makes it definite, refined by bisection [@nocedal2006numerical, Algorithm 3.3]; the dense phase
takes the absolute values of the eigenvalues instead. On a simulated alignment of 200 gels with
721 parameters (`bench/sparse/alignment.R`), 20 Gauss-Newton iterations followed by the
limited-memory phase reach the optimum of Gauss-Newton from every start, at 20 to 70 times the
median time of Gauss-Newton: with $B_0$ fixed the phase converges linearly, and every step solves with $2m$ more low-rank
columns. Gauss-Newton stays the source of a sparse fit; the BFGS phase is for objectives whose
Gauss-Newton Hessian misses curvature that matters.

## L1 penalties

`trustL1()` minimizes the objective plus an L1 penalty on some of the parameters
[@tibshirani1996regression],

$$\ell(\theta) + \sum_{i \in P} \lambda_i \lvert \theta_i - \mu_i \rvert , \tag{19}$$

with penalized parameters $P$, references $\mu_i$ and strengths $\lambda_i$. `trustL1()` runs the
trust region with the Gauss-Newton Hessian and two changes: a parameter on the kink is removed from
(1) while $\lvert \partial \ell / \partial \theta_i \rvert \le \lambda_i$, and a step across the kink is
cut back onto $\mu_i$, so zero differences are exact. Further penalties are a one-sided one,

$$\lambda_i \max(0,\, \mu_i - \theta_i) , \tag{20}$$

which keeps a parameter on the kink while $0 \le \partial \ell / \partial \theta_i \le \lambda_i$; a gate
$\lambda_i (\theta_i - \mu_i)$ with $\theta_i \ge \mu_i$, which keeps it there while
$\partial \ell / \partial \theta_i \ge -\lambda_i$; and a [fused block]{#def-fused-block} $B$, the [clustered lasso]{#def-clustered-lasso}
[@hauber2023uncovering] in the L1 form (Hauber et al. favor the exponent 0.8),

$$\lambda \sum_{p < q \in B} w_{pq}\, \lvert \theta_p - \theta_q \rvert , \tag{21}$$

optionally with an anchor; it merges the parameters of $B$ into clusters of equal value, which move
as one until the data split them.

## Forward and reverse derivatives on the Oppelt fit

Each source needs other derivatives ([Sensitivities and Hessians](methods-sensitivities.html)):

| source | derivatives per evaluation | sweep |
|---|---|---|
| Gauss-Newton | value, gradient and $J^\top L J$ from the forward sensitivities, one tangent per parameter | forward |
| BFGS, SR1 | value and gradient; the gradient from one backward sweep of the adjoint system | reverse |
| exact | value, gradient and exact Hessian by forward over reverse | reverse, `deriv2 = TRUE` |

Seconds per evaluation of the data term at the best fit, minimum of ten, from `sensitivities.R`:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
invisible(stored(file.path(oppelt, "results", "sensitivities.rds"),
                 file.path(oppelt, "sensitivities.R"), envir = new.env()))
```

```{r}
timing <- readRDS(file.path(oppelt, "results", "sensitivities.rds"))$timing
timing
```

`optimizers.R` fits from the same 100 prior draws with the default of `trust()`, Gauss-Newton, BFGS and SR1 on the reverse
gradient from the identity, the exact Hessian, 20 Gauss-Newton iterations followed by BFGS, and the
structured methods of [Structured secant updates](#structured-secant-updates), with and without
residual scaling and the shift of the hybrids; a draw without a stable resting state is replaced
by one with, and a task runs at most 30 minutes:

```{r optimizers, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
invisible(stored(file.path(oppelt, "results", "optimizers.rds"),
                 file.path(oppelt, "optimizers.R"), envir = new.env()))
```

```{r}
opt <- readRDS(file.path(oppelt, "results", "optimizers.rds"))
opt$method <- factor(opt$method, unique(opt$method))
top <- min(opt$value, na.rm = TRUE)
summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(opt, opt$method), function(d) data.frame(
  starts = nrow(d), failed = sum(is.na(d$value)), converged = sum(d$converged),
  hits = sum(d$value < top + 5, na.rm = TRUE), iterations = median(d$iterations, na.rm = TRUE),
  iterlim = sum(d$iterations >= 1000, na.rm = TRUE), seconds = round(median(d$elapsed, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
  secondsPerHit = round(sum(d$elapsed, na.rm = TRUE) / max(1, sum(d$value < top + 5, na.rm = TRUE))))))
summary
```

Medians over starts; a [plateau]{#def-plateau} is a group of fits with one final value, a local
optimum; a [hit]{#def-hit} ends within 5 of the best value; `iterlim` counts the runs stopped by
the iteration limit; `failed` counts runs without result, which the time limit of a task ended. The stops by method, with a
stagnation that ends away from a stationary point of the model counted apart:

```{r}
stop <- ifelse(is.na(opt$stopReason), "failed", opt$stopReason)
stop[stop == "stagnation" & !opt$converged] <- "stagnation, not converged"
stops <- c("gradient", "fvalue", "preddiff", "stagnation", "stagnation, not converged", "radius",
           "iterlim", "failed")
table(opt$method, factor(stop, stops))
```

```{r, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 11}
plotValues(split(opt, opt$method), pseudoLog = TRUE) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
best <- function(column, fun = which.max) rownames(summary)[fun(summary[[column]])]
iterationsSR1 <- median(opt$iterations[opt$method == "SR1" & opt$converged])
```

A reverse gradient costs about 1/`r round(timing[["forward"]] / timing[["reverse"]])` of the
forward sensitivities, an exact Hessian by forward over reverse about
`r round(timing[["forward-reverse"]] / timing[["forward"]])` times. `r best("hits")` reaches the
lowest plateaus most often, `r best("converged")` converges most often, and
`r best("secondsPerHit", which.min)` needs the least time per hit.

The switch to BFGS once the radius stays unchanged for 25 or 50 iterations
([Hessian phases](#hessian-phases)) reaches as many low plateaus as the switch after 20 Gauss-Newton
iterations, at almost twice the time per hit: on this objective the radius seldom stays unchanged
that long, and the Gauss-Newton phase, with forward sensitivities on every step, does most of the
descent.

The default, the hybrid of Fides with the switch at 20 iterations of unchanged radius, converges
from more starts than Gauss-Newton and reaches as many low plateaus, at about the same time per
hit. Half of the default runs end in the Gauss-Newton phase on the value stop, which
`onStop = "end"` makes final, and the BFGS phase takes the forward gradient of the Gauss-Newton phase.

The structured methods spend a forward Gauss-Newton Hessian on every step. `"gnsbfgs"` needs the
fewest iterations of all methods, and SR1 on the residual-scaled correction converges from more
starts than any method but the exact Hessian. The shift of the hybrids by
$\rho\, I$ helps nowhere here: far from the minimum $\rho$ is large, the shifted Gauss-Newton
branch of `"gnsbfgs"` takes short steps, and most runs end at the iteration limit;
`"gnssr1"` ends where it ends without the shift.

The runs that do not converge have three causes:

- The Gauss-Newton runs at the iteration limit end on plateaus 100 to 1000 above the best value,
  with a slow oscillating mode at the onset of the stability ramp. There the Gauss-Newton model of
  the data term, which lacks the curvature of the residuals, predicts about 1.5 times the decrease
  that follows: steps are accepted, the radius stays between `1e-4` and `5e-3`, and the value
  falls by about `2e-4` per step. The exact Hessian and the BFGS phase after 20 Gauss-Newton
  iterations converge from 13 of these 15 starts.
- SR1 from the identity builds the curvature of a Hessian whose eigenvalues span six orders of
  magnitude over hundreds of rejected and accepted steps; a converged SR1 run takes a median of
  `r iterationsSR1` iterations, so `iterlim = 1000` ends the slower runs before convergence.
- On poor plateaus the value of the Oppelt objective scatters by about `2e-4` with the step-size
  control of the ODE solver, above `ftol`. A run there ends on stagnation, five rejected steps in a
  row, and counts as converged only where the full Newton step of the model predicts at most
  `mtol` ([Termination criteria](#termination-criteria)).

The stability term rises on a ramp a tenth of the inverse time span of the data wide, about
`2.8e-4` per minute (`model.R`). On a ramp of $10^{-6}$ times
the largest eigenvalue modulus, about `2e-5` here, the model of a step sees the boundary only after
the step crosses it, and the runs creep along the boundary between rejected steps
([Methods > Steady states](methods-steady-states.html#stability)). The Hessian of the stability term is the
Gauss-Newton one for every source, also for the exact Hessian.
